generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport, presentations take several forms, and each is assessed for something different. A conference-style talk on a study rewards a clear line of argument and good timing; a research poster rewards a sharp visual summary that invites questions; a group presentation on a topic rewards coordination across the team. Different subjects lean on different evidence, from lab data in sport science to session observations in coaching. The first move is the same across the school: read the brief and marking criteria so you know which skills this format is really testing, then prepare for that rather than for a presentation in general.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport and exercise science students are set the same task: a ten-minute presentation on a study, assessed against a marking brief.

Tom prepares the way he always does: a full set of slides, every point written out, and a plan to read through them. The content is sound, but Tom has not checked what the brief rewards or how long the slot really is. On the day the talk overruns, the slides are dense with method detail, and the marker sees preparation but little judgement. This is a default approach applied to every format.

Amara starts with the brief and the criteria. The format is a short individual talk that rewards a clear argument and timing, so she cuts to three points, builds slides that prompt rather than script, and rehearses to time. The content is no deeper, but it fits the format, and the delivery lands. This is adapting to the task.

Both students knew their physiology. Only Amara read the format and the brief, and prepared for the presentation actually being asked for.
generatedProse.summary: Delivering a presentation well in the School of Sport begins before you speak, with reading the format and the brief. A talk, a poster and a group presentation reward different things, so the first move is to ask what this one is testing and prepare for that. You can now match a format to what its brief rewards and adapt your preparation to fit. The next lesson builds the structure and visual aids that carry a delivery.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that Tom did not?

items.text: She read the brief and format, then adapted her preparation to fit them.
She prepared more slides and wrote out every point.
She chose a longer time slot for the talk.
She used the same approach she always uses.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara read the brief and format and adapted her preparation to fit.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara did differently with the brief and the format.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara read the brief and format and adapted her preparation. More slides, a longer slot or a default approach are not what made the difference.
